checks.claim: Key: a typical plate moves a few centimetres a year
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'rates of a few centimeters per year', 'typically ranging from 1 to 10 cm per year'.

checks.claim: GPS on bedrock measures plate motion year after year
checks.note: USGS: GPS measures crustal motion 'within a fraction of a millimeter per year'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: less than a millimetre, a few metres, a few hundred metres
checks.note: Wikipedia: typical motion 'zero to 10 cm annually'; the fastest (Nazca) about 160 mm a year. None of the three is a typical yearly rate.

checks.claim: Context: about 1 to 10 cm a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow
checks.note: USGS: 'roughly at the same rate that your fingernails grow'. Grokipedia gives 1 to 10 cm.

checks.claim: Context arithmetic: 5 cm a year for a million years = 50 km
Stem: plates many wider than a continent, roughly 100 km thick
checks.note: Grokipedia: brittle layer 'approximately 100 km thick on average', lithosphere 50-200 km. The Pacific and North American plates are far larger than any continent.

checks.claim: Key: 'Slow currents of hot rock deep in the mantle' keep the plates moving
checks.note: Grokipedia does call mantle convection 'the primary mechanism driving plate tectonics', so the key is the defensible best choice. But its wording (currents of HOT rock DEEP in the mantle) paints the old conveyor-belt / basal-drag picture. Wikipedia: 'the asthenosphere is insufficiently competent or rigid to directly cause motion by friction', and slab pull 'is therefore most widely thought to be the greatest force acting on the plates'. Fix: key 'Slow churning of hot and cold rock in the mantle' (covers rising hot rock and the sinking cold plate edges).

checks.claim: Context: the sinking cold edge of a plate 'helps drag the plate along'
checks.note: Understates it to the point of reversing the ranking. Grokipedia Mantle convection: plate velocities are 'driven primarily by subduction', slab pull '50-70% of plate motion'; Grokipedia Plate tectonics: slab pull 'approximately 70% of the total driving force', ridge push 'typically 5-10% of slab pull's effect'; Grokipedia Mid-ocean ridge: slab pull 60-80%, ridge push 20-40%; Wikipedia: slab pull 'the greatest force acting on the plates'. Also 'the plates move with it' makes plates passengers, when they are the cold top of the churning. Fix: '...hot rock rising and cooler rock sinking. The plates are the cold top of that churning: where a plate's old, cold edge sinks back into the mantle, its weight drags the rest of the plate along, and geologists think this pull is the strongest force of all; the high, hot ridges where plates are made give a smaller push.'

checks.claim: Context: mantle heat mostly from radioactive atoms and heat left from Earth's birth; mantle is solid rock that churns
checks.note: Grokipedia: radiogenic about 50%, secular (primordial) cooling about 40%, core about 10%; 'the slow, creeping motion of the Earth's solid silicate mantle'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: Earth's spin and the Moon's tides too weak
checks.note: Grokipedia: Jeffreys calculated Wegener's tidal forces 'orders of magnitude too weak'; the polar-fleeing force from rotation likewise rejected. (A tidal-drag idea survives only as a contested fringe proposal, per Wikipedia.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the Sun's heat warms only the ground near the surface
checks.note: Seasonal swings die out within roughly 10-25 m; below that heat comes from inside the Earth.

checks.claim: Key: ocean plate sinks because its rock is denser than continental rock
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the denser oceanic plate sinks into the mantle beneath the less dense plate'; continental crust is more felsic and buoyant. USGS This Dynamic Earth says the same.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it is thicker and heavier than the continent
checks.note: Ocean crust (about 5-10 km) and ocean lithosphere (50-100 km) are thinner than continental crust (about 35 km) and lithosphere (100-200 km). Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: weight of sea presses it down; it is hotter and softer
checks.note: Oceanic lithosphere sinks as it cools and thickens with age; cold, not hot, and not because of the water.

checks.claim: Context: grows colder and denser with age; thinner crust; a trench where it bends down
checks.note: Grokipedia: oceanic lithosphere sinks as it cools and thickens with age; trenches form where the plate bends down.

checks.claim: Key: curved active island chain beside a deep trench = one plate sinking beneath another
checks.note: Grokipedia: island arc is 'a curved chain of volcanic islands and seamounts formed above a subduction zone' that 'typically parallel deep oceanic trenches'; arcs 'collectively host over 250 active volcanoes'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: pulling apart, hot spot, sliding past
checks.note: Hot-spot chains are distinct, intraplate, age-ordered, no trench; divergent and transform boundaries build no trench-side arc.

checks.claim: Context: water carried down helps the hot rock above melt
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'volatiles released from the dehydrating slab' lower the melting point of the mantle wedge above.

checks.claim: Context: on a hot-spot chain only the youngest volcanoes, at one end, are active
checks.note: USGS HVO's active list (Kilauea, Mauna Loa, Hualalai, Mauna Kea, Haleakala, Kama'ehuakanaloa) all lie on the two youngest islands at the south-east end, so 'the youngest volcanoes, at one end' holds.

checks.claim: Key: continent-continent collision raises a range of high mountains
checks.note: Grokipedia: crust shortens and thickens into mountain belts (Himalayas).

checks.claim: Context: continental rock too light to sink far, so neither continent goes under
checks.note: USGS: 'When two continents meet head-on, neither is subducted because the continental rocks are relatively light'. Grokipedia adds that Indian lithosphere is underthrust beneath Tibet and some continental crust reaches 100-150 km before returning; 'too light to sink far' keeps the child-level line true. Optional tightening: 'neither continent sinks deep into the mantle'.

checks.claim: Context: crust thickens to about twice its usual thickness
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'initial crustal thicknesses of around 35 km have doubled to approximately 70 km'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice / context: arc volcanoes die out, no trench left
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the cessation of arc volcanism'; collision gives distributed deformation 'rather than localized trench dynamics'. A little later potassic magmatism occurs, but no volcano chain.

checks.claim: Context: the Himalayas still being pushed higher today
checks.note: Grokipedia: India-Asia converge about 4-5 cm a year; GPS uplift about 2 mm a year at Everest.

checks.claim: Stem: the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain chain on Earth
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the longest mountain chain on Earth', about 65,000 km.

checks.claim: Key: magma fills the gap and hardens into new sea floor
checks.note: Grokipedia: decompression melting at 30-100 km depth; magma rises, cools and makes basaltic new crust.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: seawater open crack, settling mud and sand, broken rock from the edges
checks.note: None fills the gap; new crust is igneous rock from rising magma.

checks.claim: Context: ridge stands high because new rock is hot and swollen, not squeezed up
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'thermal expansion that elevates the seafloor by up to 2-3 km'; SERC lists ridges from 'uplift or convergence' as a misconception.

checks.claim: Key: a continental rift that keeps spreading becomes the floor of a new ocean
checks.note: Grokipedia: divergence can 'lead to the formation of new ocean basins if divergence persists over millions of years'.

checks.claim: Context: the Red Sea is a young ocean opening this way
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a young continental rift in transition toward oceanic spreading'; Augustin et al. 2021 (Nature Communications): sea-floor spreading along the whole Red Sea since about 13 million years ago, normal oceanic crust. 'Young ocean' fits both.

checks.claim: Context: East African rift valleys may one day become an ocean
checks.note: Grokipedia: Afar is 'progressively developing into an oceanic spreading center'; 'may' is properly hedged.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: trench, folded mountains, transform fault
checks.note: Trenches and folded ranges belong to convergence, sliding faults to transforms; none is what a widening rift becomes.

checks.claim: Key: old sea floor sinks back into the mantle, balancing new floor
checks.note: Grokipedia: crust production at spreading centres 'matches the consumption at subduction zones'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth swells larger (expanding Earth)
checks.note: Rejected; no measurable expansion.

checks.claim: Context: 2011 satellite measurements found no growth beyond about 0.1 mm a year, statistically insignificant
checks.note: JPL, Aug. 16, 2011 (Xiaoping Wu): average change 'about 0.004 inches (0.1 millimeters) per year', 'statistically insignificant'. Methods were satellite laser ranging, GPS, GRACE and VLBI (VLBI uses radio telescopes, not satellites); 'satellite measurements' is a fair summary.

checks.claim: Context: some geologists once argued Earth is swelling
checks.note: Mantovani, Hilgenberg, S. W. Carey (geologist) and others.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: crust stretched thinner everywhere; waves grind sea floor to sand
checks.note: Neither accounts for the new crust; it is recycled at subduction zones.

checks.claim: Stem: 1906 fence offset about 2.6 m
checks.note: USGS: G. K. Gilbert's photo near Bolinas shows 'a fence that was offset about 8.5 feet along the trace of the fault' (8.5 ft = 2.59 m). Other fences moved more (up to 20 ft near Point Reyes), but the stem says only 'a fence', so the figure stands.

checks.claim: Key: the fault stuck while stress built, then slipped (elastic rebound)
checks.note: Grokipedia: the fault 'remains locked, preventing slip and allowing stresses to build over decades to centuries', rock deforms elastically and stores energy until release.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: plates stood still for years then lurched
checks.note: GPS shows plates move steadily; it is the locked fault, not the plates, that sticks. SERC/M5 misconception.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: rising magma pushed sides apart; underground hollow caved in
checks.note: The San Andreas is a transform fault, 'rarely associated with volcanism'; collapse of hollows is an old explanation.

checks.claim: Context: Harry Fielding Reid worked out elastic rebound from the 1906 ground movement
checks.note: Grokipedia: Reid, 1908 report and 1910 publication, from 1906 fault offsets compared with earlier Coast and Geodetic Survey triangulation.

checks.claim: Key: next island rises just south-east of the active island
checks.note: Grokipedia: Kama'ehuakanaloa, the youngest edifice of the chain, lies about 35 km south-east of Hawai'i; summit about 975 m below sea level.

checks.claim: Direction and age order: plate moves north-west; islands older toward the north-west; oldest drowned
checks.note: USGS: islands 'systematically increase in age towards the west-northwest', plate 'carries each volcano towards the west-northwest'; 'north-west' is a fair child-level rounding. Older volcanoes subside and drown as seamounts (Grokipedia Hotspot).

checks.claim: Context: hot spot stays nearly still while the plate moves
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'relatively fixed' hot spot.

checks.claim: Context: about 35 km south-east of the island of Hawaii
checks.note: Grokipedia 35 km; USGS HVO says about 30 km. 'About 35' is fine.

checks.claim: Stem: only the island at the south-east end has active volcanoes
checks.note: The stem's chain is generic, but the context makes Hawaii the example, and for Hawaii it is not true: USGS HVO lists Haleakala on Maui as active ('the only active volcano on the Island of Maui, erupted most recently between about 600 and 400 years ago'). The answer is unaffected. Fix: 'Only the youngest island, at the south-east end, still erupts often.'

checks.claim: Key: the belts trace the edges of Earth's plates
checks.note: Grokipedia: plate boundaries host 'about 90% of earthquakes'.

checks.claim: Most volcanoes lie at plate edges
checks.note: USGS CVO: 'Volcanoes occur most frequently at plate boundaries'; most are at spreading ridges and subduction zones, hot spots the exception. Grokipedia: Ring of Fire about 75% of volcanoes.

checks.claim: Context: about 81 percent of the largest earthquakes in the belt around the Pacific
checks.note: USGS: circum-Pacific belt, 'about 81 percent of our planet's largest earthquakes'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: edges of the continents
checks.note: SERC misconception: 'The edge of a continent is the same thing as a plate boundary.' The Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Alpide belt are not continent edges; Atlantic coasts are quiet passive margins (Grokipedia Passive margin).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: rivers of magma; wrinkles on a shrinking Earth
checks.note: Magma is not a layer of rivers (SERC: 'Asthenosphere is liquid' misconception); the contracting-Earth hypothesis was superseded by plate tectonics.

checks.claim: Context: 1800s geologists explained mountain belts as wrinkles on a cooling, shrinking Earth, like a drying apple
checks.note: A Dictionary of Earth Sciences: prevalent in the 19th and early 20th centuries; 'the wrinkles that form on a drying apple' as the analogy.

checks.claim: Context: 'but the belts follow the plates' edges instead' (said of mountain belts)
checks.note: The sentence's 'belts' are the mountain belts, and old ranges such as the Appalachians and Urals now sit inside plates (they mark plate edges of the past). Mountains 'mainly result from plate tectonic motions', but not all follow today's edges. Fix: 'but young mountain belts, like the earthquake belts, follow the plates' edges instead.'

unit_notes: Checked 2026-11-26, Grokipedia first, then USGS, JPL, Wikipedia. Speeds (1-10 cm a year, fingernail rate), the 1906 fence (8.5 ft = 2.6 m, Gilbert, Bolinas), hot-spot direction and age order, the 81 percent figure and the 2011 JPL result all check out. The one real error is the driving force in d8c219c10d: every source rates slab pull the largest force (about 50-80 percent) and ridge push small, but the context calls the sinking edge only a helper to deep hot currents. Two minor wording points: Haleakala on Maui counts as active (6669574224), and old mountain belts lie inside plates (51db9da9bd).
